title: Astrea guide

about.title: About Astrea
about.description: We are the team behind Astrea, a project for exploring the sky and real SPHEREx images. We combine software development, data analysis, interface design, infrastructure and project coordination to make astronomical data more accessible.
about.profile: {{name}} on GitHub (opens in a new tab)
about.repositoryDescription: Explore the source code and development of Astrea on GitHub.

intro.title: Welcome to Astrea
intro.summary: Explore the sky and discover real images from SPHEREx, a space telescope that observes infrared light, invisible to our eyes.
intro.sky: Drag to look around the sky and use the mouse wheel to zoom in or out.
intro.images: Choose a region and see images taken by the telescope.
intro.compare: Alternate between images from different dates to look for possible changes.
intro.spectrum: Explore how bright a point in the sky is in different parts of infrared light.
intro.note: You do not need experience in astronomy. The guide takes you through an example you can try, step by step.

welcome.title: Explore Astrea
welcome.summary: Let's explore the region around Barnard's Star with real images. The highlighted area shows which part of the screen you can try.

1.title: Find your way around the controls
1.description: The icons on the left open the sky options. Click Next to get to know them.

2.title: Try things at your own pace
2.description: You can change the example's settings. When you leave, your session from before the guide will return.

welcome.note: Move forward or back at your own pace. Leave with Skip all and open the guide again from the question mark icon.

time.title: Sky time
time.summary: The sky shifts as the hours pass. This clock chooses the moment you are viewing, without changing when each image was taken.

1.title: See the sky as it is now
1.description: Click Return to current time. Use Pause time to keep that moment fixed.

2.title: Travel to another moment
2.description: Choose a date and time, then click Apply date to see how the sky changes.

time.note: Times use UTC, a worldwide reference that may differ from your local time. The example starts with the clock paused.

location.title: Observer location
location.summary: Choose where on Earth you are viewing the sky from. This lets Astrea place the stars and images in the corresponding direction.

1.title: Check the starting location
1.description: This example starts in Greenwich, United Kingdom. This does not mean we have detected your location.

2.title: Try another place
2.description: Use device location, or enter latitude and longitude and click Apply manual location.

location.note: Latitude and longitude describe a place on Earth. If you prefer to leave them as they are, you can continue with Greenwich.

search.title: Find the Barnard region
search.summary: Preparation lets you choose which part of the sky to view. RA and Dec are its address in the sky; Barnard's is already filled in.

1.title: Start with this example
1.description: Keep RA, Dec and the size of 7 arcminutes: that size describes how much sky the image covers.

2.title: Open the image
2.description: Click Search coordinates. You will see the image over the sky and its options in the right panel.

search.note: The guide loads this example if you move on without searching. Outside the guide, you can also choose a region by clicking the sky.

sky.title: Sky appearance
sky.summary: These options change the surrounding sky, where the images you explore are placed.

1.title: Try a guide for orientation
1.description: Turn on Show central surface: the grid provides a horizontal reference beneath your feet.

2.title: Choose the background you prefer
2.description: Toggle Diffuse background to see the sky with or without that visual effect.

sky.note: The diffuse background is an illustration. The telescope images are real data, which you can explore in the right panel.

data.title: Data
data.summary: Each observation is an image taken by the telescope at a particular time. Data helps you identify the one you are looking at.

1.title: See when it was taken
1.description: Check the date. D3 identifies the detector that took it; each detector observes a part of the infrared range.

2.title: Find the image again
2.description: Click Center image to bring it into the middle of your view and see the whole image.

data.note: You do not need to understand the technical data to explore. Open original FITS gives you access to the image's scientific file.

appearance.title: Appearance
appearance.summary: Adjust the image to make its details easier to see. You can try these controls without changing the telescope's original file.

1.title: Find a look that helps you
1.description: Try another palette or adjust the brightness. Lower the opacity to see the sky behind the image too.

2.title: Start again if you need to
2.description: Click Reset appearance to return to the initial settings.

appearance.note: Colors show how bright each region is; they are not its real colors. You can leave the Processing options for later.

compare.title: Compare
compare.summary: Look at the same region at different times. Alternating between images makes possible differences easier to notice.

1.title: Find another date for this region
1.description: Keep the year 2025 and the same D3 detector. The image you already opened becomes reference A.

2.title: Add the second image
2.description: Click Add beside the other available observation. Outside the guide, you can keep adding more.

3.title: Move through the images
3.description: Drag the timeline or click Play to alternate between them. Time per image controls the speed.

compare.note: These two images were taken 6.6 hours apart. You may not see any motion; a visual difference alone does not confirm it either.

spectrum.title: Spectrum
spectrum.summary: Spectrum shows how bright a point in the sky is at different wavelengths: different parts of infrared light.

1.title: Load the example measurements
1.description: Keep PSF fit, the initial method for measuring stars, and click D3 within Spectrum.

2.title: Read the chart
2.description: Wavelength changes from left to right. The higher a point sits, the greater the measured brightness.

3.title: Explore each measurement
3.description: Point to a dot to see its date, brightness and margin of error. Each dot comes from one observation.

spectrum.note: The example measures a point near Barnard in two D3 images. Outside the guide, you can enable other detectors; loading may take a while.
